utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those following these proceedings. We turn, briefly, into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other matters to be addressed before the next witness is coming in? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Yes, there is one matter that may help the overall administrative of justice, not just for our case but for the Karadzic case as well. I have been informed that the Karadzic Defence has made a request for confidential material in our case, which, as you know, is part of the ongoing process. I believe they -- they are looking for the testimony of 208 who partially testified in public, as you know, recently, and we have filed our notice of compliance and not objected to that. And we just did it this afternoon. Apparently, the Prosecution in Karadzic would really like to be able to get the Defence their request because there may be some Rule 68, that kind of thing, and there are some witnesses that are coming up where the Defence really would like to have it. And so it's my understanding that if we can get from General Tolimir his view on whether he and Mr. Gajic have any problems with that material being released per the procedures, that should be able to free it up if he doesn't. If he does, of course, then that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I take it that this relates to a decision of this Chamber filed last year that the Defence in the Karadzic case may be -- have access to confidential material in our case, and indeed we asked the parties to update the Chamber on a monthly basis to -- about the progress in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is our second notice, and my memory of this is that perhaps you had to remind us a time or two to do this so -- but, yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is absolutely where this is coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, what is your position in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Greetings to everyone present here. And peace unto this courtroom, and let the outcome of this trial be decided by providence rather than by my wishes. The Defence has no objection to any disclosure whatsoever, and since this is a Prosecution witness, it is up to them to decide. We didn't even have any questions for that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, I think, not quite correct because both parties have to agree on this kind of disclosure of confidential material and we asked both parties, that means also the Defence, to update us on a monthly basis. But I take it this is now your agreement with this disclosure at this point in time. This is now on the record, but I expect you to file such submissions and notices to the Chamber on a monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Registry will provide the Defence in the Karadzic case with the relevant material. Any other matters to be dealt with before the witness is coming in? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has only one oral submission, pursuant to 65 ter Rule. It concerns a document that we have received just now over the weekend from the witness himself during the proofing session. It is a document uploaded in e-court under number 1D111, 65 ter 1D111. There is one digit missing. There should be four 1s. 1D1111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it on the record. Can you -- and you said it is uploaded in e-court and it's available to the Prosecution, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. It is available to the Prosecution, too. Unfortunately, we don't have a translation into English since we received this document over the weekend. This concerns the notes that the witness made during the relevant period during the war, and we believe that it contains relevant information that will be of assistance to the Trial Chamber to reach a proper decision, and we are going to use this document during the examination of this witness. We are also going to give the CLSS some time to translate at least one portion of this document or -- but I don't believe that we shall be able to question this witness about it today. Therefore, we are kindly asking the leave of the Chamber to allow us to add this one document to our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have not seen it yet, Mr. President, but no, not at all. That's, of course, normally happens all the time here and we have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then leave is granted to add this document, 1D1111, to the Defence 65 ter exhibit list. Anything else to be dealt with now? Since this is not the case, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Skrbic. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Defence, that means Mr. Tolimir, is now conducting his examination-in-chief, followed by the Prosecution. Did you receive a proper interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please commence your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Greetings to Mr. Skrbic and I wish him a pleasant stay here with us. I have a few questions for him. Can you please tell us your full name, for the record? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also tell us, for the record, what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 20th of October, 1946, in Glamoc, in the People's Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was part at the time of the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia. My birthplace was unfortunately burned in 1995, and my parent's house is no longer there. This is where I finished my elementary school, then I went to the teacher's college, and then a military academy. At the moment, I am retired and I am mostly engaged in scientific research work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but that was a very simple question of his occupation and he offered a whole lot of details about the burning of his house and things, so I would hope that we can direct the witness to try to answer the question; otherwise, this is going to be quite a long day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was going to do the same to give some guidance in that respect, but I didn't want to do that after the first question of the witness -- put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic, for your answer. My next question is as follows: Have you ever testified before this Tribunal, and if you have, in which cases? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I have testified before this Tribunal on two occasions. For the first time it was in Popovic et al. case, and for the second time it was in the Perisic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you appear in the Popovic et al. case as a Defence witness or a Prosecution witness? And the same question applies to the Perisic case as well.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In the Popovic et al. case I was a Prosecution witness, and in the Perisic case I was a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, briefly, something about your educational background? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I finished elementary school in my birthplace in the village of Hotkovci in Glamoc. I started attending teacher's college in Livno for one year, and I finished it in Banja Luka in 1965. I had scholarship granted by the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. When I finished the teacher's college, I went to the military academy in Belgrade. I attended a general course there for two years, then one semester I spent in Zadar, and after that I returned to Batajnica, near Belgrade, where I finished rocket missile school in 1968. In --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the year, again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you. I have to stop you for a moment. The interpreters didn't catch part of your answer, especially in relation to a year. The last sentence you started was: "I attended a general course there for two years, then one semester I spent in Zadar, and after that I returned to Batajnica, near Belgrade, where I finished rocket missile school in 1968 ..." From there on, please, repeat what you have said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to repeat, Your Honours. I understand your question. This rocket missile school was part of the anti-aircraft defence course, and I finished it in 1968. Then in 1978 I finished high military and political school. In 1983 I acquired an MA at the faculty of political sciences, and my thesis was: "Freedom as the Meaning and Essence of the Defence of a Society."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, if I may ask you to try and speak more slowly for the benefit of the interpreters. I will do my best to do the same because both of us speak the same language and this is causing problems for them. Thank you. Now, please, can you tell us when did you become a member of the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 17th December, 1993. Your Honours, earlier I gave a statement in which I said that I became a member on the 17th November, 1993. I don't know whether that was my mistake or somebody else's mistake. I would, anyway, like this to be corrected. So the correct date is the 17th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Can you please tell the Chamber something about your career prior to 1993 when you joined the Army of Republika Srpska on the 17th of December? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: After I finished military academy, I was assigned to the 1st Rocket Battalion of the 205th [as interpreted] Rocket Regiment in Batajnica. I worked there as a technician involved in creating commands. Maybe this is incomprehensible for you, but I have to tell you what the title of my job was at the time. After that I was transferred to the rocket brigade command in Belgrade, where I discharged the duties of a commander and, at the same time, I was the chief of the operations centre of the 205th [as interpreted] Operational Regiment. After that, I was an assistant of the division commander for political guidance until 1977. As I said, in that year I started attending the school, as I already indicated, which I finished in 1979. In this high political school of the JNA, following its completion, I taught the subject which was called dialectical philosophy of society [as interpreted]. I remained in that post until 1985. In the meantime, General Tolimir also finished a course as an attendee in the high political school which means that I was one of his teachers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, unfortunately, it seems that we have a couple of mistakes in the transcript. First page 9, lines 19 and 24. I think that I heard the witness say "250th" not "205th" or "2005th."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I noticed that there were different ways to record it, and therefore I would kindly ask you to say -- to give us the correct number of this regiment again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exact designation number is 250th, 250, Rocket Regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think now we have it on the record correctly. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, and on page 10, line 4, the translation says "dialectical philosophy of society," and it should read, according to what the witness says, "the dialectics of society or philosophy." So there is no equation between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This might be an interpretation issue. Could you please, again, sir, tell us, you taught the subject which was called, and now again this subject, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The subject was called the dialectics of society.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how your career progressed from that moment onwards? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: From that moment on, I was assigned to the political administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. I was an officer in charge of idealogical and political guidance of JNA officers. Later, I was assigned as official for scientific and research work in the field of social sciences, that was in the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. When the JNA -- I apologise, I've remembered other duties that I performed and perhaps it's relevant. After my duties as an official for scientific research, I was assigned to an analytical group which was involved in analysing and dealing with the JNA and All People's Defence, and this was within the framework of public information, within the framework of the media. After the JNA was transformed into the Army of Yugoslavia, which was in 1992, I was assigned to the administration for morale in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia as the chief of the 1st Department for Morale, therefore for moral guidance. And three months prior to the completion of my duties in the Army of Yugoslavia, I performed the duties of the director of military editorial centre of the Army of Yugoslavia. It was also a publishing group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please inform the Chamber whether anyone forced you to go to the Army of Republika Srpska? And could you briefly tell us about the circumstances under which you became a member of the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No one forced me to join the Army of Republika Srpska. As for the circumstances, as I was involved in analytical work, I was quite familiar with the circumstances, the circumstances were such that the circumstances themselves put pressure on -- on a man and on one's reason. Then it was also often said that those who were there should defend their homeland, the place they were born in, and in my opinion that's quite correct. And in 1992 I wanted to go to Republika Srpska. However, the chief of the General Staff, General Zivota Panic prevented me from doing so, because I was forced to carry out an analysis for the General Staff. And then, thus, in 1993, I decided to go to the Army of Republika Srpska. That was in 1993 and I went there. You already have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, when you arrived in the Army of Republika Srpska, when you joined it, what rank did you have and what establishment position did you have?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: When I joined the Army of Republika Srpska, my rank was that of a colonel. I had to perform the duties of an assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs in the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us which duties you performed, if they were numerous, within the 2nd Krajina Corps? Thank you. I am referring to the duties you had to perform as an assistant for religious and legal affairs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I've understood your question, Mr. Tolimir. Within the field of morale, the duties I performed involved gathering and analysing information on the morale of all the members of the 2nd Krajina Corps. And on that basis, I submitted a monthly report to the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, which would then be signed by the corps commander. As for religious affairs, we co-operated with the Orthodox Church. When anniversaries were held or celebrations were held in the army, there were anniversaries, consecration of buildings, of the flags of certain brigades, and there were also religious services, masses, outside the army in churches, so then we tried to see how to take members of the army to the church to see when they were free or when they weren't involved in combat activities and so on and so forth. As far as legal affairs are concerned, I had a reserve officer who was a judge in Bosnian Petrovac, a civilian judge in Bosnian Petrovac [as interpreted], and his task was to analyse and gather information on violations of discipline and on crimes. And he had to submit reports to the military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka, and that office would then decide whether to institute proceedings or not. Your Honours, I've really tried to be brief but it wasn't possible for me to be more succinct, so I do apologise if I went into some detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed we all would appreciate if you could be as short and as precise as possible. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you remain in the 2nd Corps until the end of the war, or were you also in some other unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I didn't remain in the 2nd Krajina Corps until the end, but in July 1994 I was transferred to the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what your establishment position was in the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. We are getting a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- a translation that is "the General Staff," and I just -- I don't know if he's saying "general" or "glavni." And I know they know the difference but I just want to point that out because there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please clarify the right term with the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, which unit did you join after you were transferred from the 2nd Krajina Corps, and what was your establishment position? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. My position was that of assistant commander of the Main Staff, responsible for organisational, mobilisation, and personnel issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. To describe your career, before we move on to other essential issues, could you tell us how long you stayed in the Army of Republika Srpska and how did your career subsequently develop? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I remained in the Army of Republika Srpska until the end of 1996. At the beginning of 1997, I was transferred to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're microphone is off, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters and to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell us which place you went to and which establishment position did you have in the Army of Yugoslavia, after you left the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you. And I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the personnel department of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and I was the assistant for the -- the assistant chief for the personnel department in the year 2000. By decree of the president of the republic, I was assigned to the deputy or the assistant chief for the administration for moral guidance, and on that very same year -- in that very same year I was the minister of defence for information. In 2001, on the 4th [as interpreted] of April, my military career came to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpretation -- interpreter's correction, I was assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order for the record, could you tell us when you retired in 2001, in which month did you retire, and what was your rank when you retired?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I retired on the 1st of April, 2001. My rank was lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Let's move on to your duties as the assistant commander for organisational matters in the Army of Republika Srpska in its Main Staff. Can you tell us where the sector for organisational and personnel issues is located, and you're a member of that body? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have the place, the location in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise, Mr. Skrbic. I am asking you about the location, the place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: All the staff who worked in the sector where I worked as an assistant was located in Han Pijesak, the rear command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us how far that was from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in kilometres, and could you tell us where the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was actually located? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was in a place called Crna Rijeka, which, in my assessment, is about 3 and a half to 4 kilometres from Han Pijesak. I apologise, Your Honours. I have to rephrase that, with your leave. It's not a place. It's not a village. It was a location of the Main Staff, but there was no settlement there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Please, could you tell us what duties you had as assistant commander for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel issues in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I had a lot of tasks that I had to carry out. I'll try to give you a general idea of these tasks and not go into all the details. That would take a lot of time. But all the duties that I performed had to do with personnel issues. It concerned managing offices. It involved training, education, promotion, cessation of activity, and so on and so forth. As for organisation, as far as organisation is concerned, we didn't have too much work because when I arrived in the Main Staff, organisational matters had been dealt with. Mobilisation -- well, the Main Staff had to draw up mobilisation plans and co-ordinate this with units. As for calling up men and obtaining supplies, that was the responsibility of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. As you said, organisational matters had been dealt with. Could you briefly tell the Chamber what organisation involves? What is involved in organisational work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Organisation is a system, and the army uses units and institutions that it sets up in order to function as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, could you tell us whether you had all the information on the structure and organisation of the Main Staff and of other units of the Army of Republika Srpska that was subordinated to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Chamber what personnel issues involves? What field does this cover? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've partially provided you with a description of those duties. I'll add something else, and this concerns something that was done together with the minister of defence of the Republika Srpska, and this had to do with publishing competitions for military schools and academies. Other forms of training were under my responsibility, right up to the level of military -- the military academy. We didn't send officers to military schools above the level of military academy, though there are such schools, because we believed that war was the best way to obtain an education. As for other activities, there was the activity of assigning professional and reserve officers or deploying them. Assigning them establishment positions, issuing orders that pertain to such establishment positions. Then we had to deal with promotional matters, promoting to the rank of major or general. A certain procedure then had to be followed, and I hope there will be questions about that because it's a different procedure for each and every category. And then there was also the matter of retirement, if necessary. I say "if necessary" because some men were wounded, some were killed. A decision on retirement would have to be taken so that the family of a person concerned could receive certain benefits, for example. So there were quite a lot of tasks, and I think I have said enough. I wouldn't want to go into too many details about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you discharge quite a few duties, can you tell us, briefly, what did you mean by mobilisation, because that was also in the name of the institution that you worked for? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It implies the submission of requests to the Ministry of Defence in order to call up conscripts and institutions to place their assets at the disposal of the VRS Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us how mobilisation is being carried out in wartime? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: There are several ways to do that. When general mobilisation is proclaimed, then men are not called up but, rather, units can freely recruit all able-bodied men and engage them in units. However, when there is no mobilisation and no state of war, then civilian organisations are the one who send out call-up papers, and they served personally to each individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether there was a state of war declared in Republika Srpska, and if it was, when was that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: A state of war was declared in Republika Srpska in the area of responsibility of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I believe that that was in early 1995. Then what followed was the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps, again in 1995, and then in the area of Srebrenica in 1995. However, a state of war in the entire territory of Republika Srpska was declared only in October 1995. I may be wrong with the months but the year is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to organisation and mobilisation and personnel duties that you discharged, did you perform any other duties? And if you did, on whose orders did you do that whilst you were in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. Of course I performed other duties as well, as per orders of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. I had no option but to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us if your department was obliged to keep precise records about organisations, structure, and level of recruitment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of our obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was the staffing level of the Main Staff compared to those envisaged in the establishment? If you have this information.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The staffing level of the Main Staff was very poor. It didn't reach 30 per cent. Some organisational units within the staff had even a lower percentage of the staffing levels.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P2227 in e-court. Thank you. It's a chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has a sufficient number of hard copies of this chart in both languages. Since the screen is too small for this kind of chart, we believe that it would be beneficial for everyone following these proceedings be given a hard copy and the witness will have a copy in the B/C/S which is in A3 format. And I think that will facilitate the whole procedure for everyone involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I appreciate that. And the Court Usher should give one copy to the witness, one to the Prosecution, and for the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter from the booth also would like to have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, do you have enough copies so that we can provide the interpreters also with a copy for every booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More than enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The interpreters should get one, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, as you can see, this is the chart that depicts the composition of the Main Staff of the VRS in July 1995. My question is: Did you have an opportunity to become familiarised with this chart as we see it here during your preparations for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We see here that it says "The commander of the Main Staff" on top, and that's Colonel General Ratko Mladic. Can you see that anything is missing there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: A box is missing there which should indicate his staff or cabinet or office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since this box is missing, can you please insert it in the chart, if you know, and mark it with a number 1, or you can orally explain who members of the commander's office were while you were there, for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's sufficient that it is explained orally because we have one technical problem: You see the screen is divided. On top we have the B/C/S version and below that the English version of this chart. That's helpful for those who can't read both languages. So it's, perhaps, more satisfying if the witness would explain orally because, otherwise, he has to put some comments or in additions to both versions on the screen. Mr. Skrbic, are you able to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, can you tell us what should be added here next to the box which says "Commander of the Main Staff" as an integral part of this organ, and just explain this to us orally?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am going to try to simplify this as much as I can, and I think that everyone listening to this will understand. So a box is missing which should indicate the office, and it is at the same level as the department for civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we see here the department for civilian affairs has two members of staff, can you tell us how many people would be in that box that is missing indicating the office of the Main Staff and who they were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: For a long time, this office box was blank, and after that we appointed Rajko Banduka who was transferred from the position of aide-de-camp, and then later on his rank was warrant officer. And then later on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the second member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the second name you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the second person was Major Dragomir Pecanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, we see here that all the sectors in this third line belonging to the Main Staff are indicated. Can you tell us what was the position of the Chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: According to this organisational chart, the box that you are asking me about, Mr. Tolimir, is correctly filled. The Chief of Staff is at the same time a deputy commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what is the difference between the commander and the Chief of Staff as his deputy, and what are his powers with regard to command and control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This formulation, Your Honours, comes from the establishment of the VRS, and it says that the Chief of Staff is, at the same time, a deputy commander of the Main Staff. According to that description, it means that the Chief of Staff stands in for the commander when he is prevented from carrying out his duties and no specific orders are needed. Other persons indicated here can only stand in for the commander pursuant to an appropriate document that can be -- only be issued by the president of the republic. In short, the Chief of Staff can act as a deputy commander at any given time but never when the commander is present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Was it possible for the commander, if he was there, to delegate certain powers with regard to command/control to the Chief of Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain, briefly, what this meant in practice in the operation of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Your Honours, was -- for example, the commander was entitled to authorise his deputy to call us to attend the senior staff meeting. We would have to respond and comply without asking whether he was authorised to do that because he would clearly be authorised. Now, as for controlling the staff units and other units, the same applied but when he was present on the premises. So he could only perform the duties that the commander gave him the authority to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, further on we see that below the commander of the Main Staff, we see assistant commanders. Can you tell the Chamber who the assistant commanders were and how many of them were on the Main Staff of the VRS in 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: According to this chart, the assistant commander positions are accurately depicted. The assistant for morale guidance, legal and religious affairs; assistant for logistics; assistant for mobilisation organisation, and personnel; assistant for intelligence and security; and the assistant for planning, development, and finances; and finally, the assistant for airforce and anti-aircraft defence. In total, Your Honours, this is six assistants. And, with your leave, I would like this to be amended because the indictment says that there were seven assistants. And I accessed the indictment on the internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is your evidence and we have it on the record. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, since you performed the duties of assistant commander for personnel affairs, could you tell us what the role of the assistant commander was in terms of control and command? What your role was, in fact?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As assistant commander for personnel, organisational, and mobilisation affairs, I had the duty of analysing the situation in the Army of Republika Srpska, and I had to prepare material for meetings that had to do with mobilisation, promotion, deployment, and the training of officers. Such material would be discussed at meetings of the commanders, but the decisions would only be taken by the commander, to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think there must be something missing, because our English says "meeting of the commanders," and I think we'll agree that there is one commander at the Main Staff, which, I think, Mr. Skrbic just said. I'm sorry to ask him, I think he needs to repeat it because it doesn't make sense the way it is in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, you have heard the last sentence by Mr. McCloskey. We see on the record, I quote: "Such material would be discussed at meetings of the commanders," plural. Can you repeat what you really said, precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. At those meetings, at those collegiums, all the corps commanders were present when the subject matter that I have just been speaking about was, in fact, discussed. So these were meetings of commanders, and the commander of the Main Staff was in charge of those meetings. He would chair those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Which commanders? It's not in the transcript. Because it's in the plural, could you reply -- could you repeat which commanders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the record. We have it on the record. He referred to the corps commanders who took part in meetings with the commander of the VRS. This is my understanding. I see the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see the witness nodding. You may continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you very briefly and precisely tell us whether the assistant commanders - and there are a number of them in this chart - could you tell us whether they had a role to play of any kind when it came to command and control? Did they have the right to command and control in the staff and in relation to the units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I apologise. All the assistant commanders in the Main Staff had the right to control but not to command. Not a single one of them had the right to command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since a distinction is made between command and control in the answer, could you tell us what command involves and what control involves? What is the distinction to be made between these two concepts in our army, in NATO, in the US, and so on and so forth? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the available literature, these concepts are both compatible and incompatible. In the West, it's a lot clearer. The term used there is "command." In the Eastern world, we have the terms "command" and "control." Sometimes the same is a meant by these two terms and sometimes a significant distinction is made. In the military schools of the JNA, there is a subject called "command and control." And the administration would be involved in analysis of control, in planning, and so on, but command involved teaching about the singleness of command and it involved teaching about tasks. But this isn't the place to discuss such scientific issues, so I think I would prefer to provide you with a practical example in order to try and explain to you what command and control actually means in the Army of Republika Srpska. In the Army of Republika Srpska, well, it is the Supreme Commander who exercises command and control. The Ministry of Defence controls some parts that fall within that domain, but in the army itself, both command and control are exercised, but only the commanders have the right to command. Only they have such authority, whereas all the others don't have such authority unless authorised, for example, unless there is an order issued by commanders authorising them. So I could say that "control" resembles a civilian process, a civilian organisation. "Command" is a military process par excellence, so that is why the term, the best and most precise term in that case is "to command."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Skrbic. This question concerning command and control is, in fact, a very complicated issue. It is something that has been frequently discussed in this courtroom. But let me come back to what you said in the transcript, page 28, line -- or lines 3 and 4. The Ministry -- the minister of defence -- the Ministry of Defence - I am trying to translate this into French - controls, or, rather has a certain amount of responsibility for control, but the army itself is responsible for command -- or command and control, in fact. Is it possible for the Ministry of Defence to control something that it has no command over? Do you have an example that you could provide us with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a little more difficult for me to hear the interpreter now. I don't know what's happening, but I understand the Honourable Judge has just said. When we are speaking about command in relation to the army, I said - and this is on the base of experience and practice, it's not a theoretical matter - the Ministry of Defence in Republika Srpska could not have command over the Army of Republika Srpska because in wartime, and it was a war, command would only be exercised under the Supreme Commander, commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. But the ministry had certain duties that it controlled, you know. Duties such as mobilisation, obtaining equipment for the army, as well as food for the army, but because it had to perform these activities, that didn't mean that it had the right to exercise command over the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down while speaking, because we lost some of your explanations on the transcript. Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's very interesting, witness. So the Ministry of Defence could, for example, exercise control over certain areas, supply, for example. But the Ministry of Defence could not exercise command. The question I am putting to myself is whether we are dealing with a semantic problem. Is it a matter of vocabulary? With regard to supplies, could you try and provide me an example to explain what command involves in relation to supplies and what control involves in relation to supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it is necessary to obtain equipment of a certain kind, then the relevant decisions are taken by the commander, that is to say, the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, and that is the president of the republic. He then assigns a task to the government. The government then forwards the task to the Ministry of Defence, which is an integral part of the government. But since it's involved -- but although it is involved in obtaining equipment and supplies, that does not mean that it has the right to exercise command over the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have understood your answer. You are quite right. But this is my last question: Could the ministry, for example, decide or order a commander to use three vehicles and afterwards could it exercise control, or did the ministry have to go along with the decision on the number of vehicles to be used if that decision was taken by the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the ministry couldn't issue orders of any kind in the course of the war. That was common practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If I may just take you back to the same quotation, but seeking a different clarification. At page 28 of today's transcript, starting from line 1, we have you recorded as stating that: "In the Army of Republika Srpska -- in the Army of Republika Srpska, well, it is the Supreme Commander who exercises command and control," and you go on up to line 8. In this passage you are using the word "commander" and "commanders" interchangeably. I am a bit confused. For example, when you say: "But in the army itself, both command and control are exercised," you don't say by who, "but only the commanders have the right to command." I assume by this you are saying assistant commanders or corps commanders. And then you go on to say: "Unless there is an order issued by commanders authorising them." Again, I am not quite sure which segment of the commanders you are referring to. I wonder if you could clarify that particular portion of your evidence for me again, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, some concepts are clear to me and I do speak rapidly, but I am surprised, however, that such confusion has been caused. I'll try and be more precise. Within the army itself, only commanders can exercise command. We start with the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, who has command over corps commanders. So the corps commanders exercise command over all the units within their corps. The brigade commanders exercise command over the brigades. The other members of the command don't have the right to exercise a command, but they do have to deal or, rather, perform the duties they are responsible for. They have to perform analysis. They have to propose measures to be taken by their commanders. For example, we would also propose measures to be taken to the commander of the Main Staff, but they also have to report on the implementation of the measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would suggest that this is a convenient time for our first break. We will resume after half an hour at 4.15. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, a moment ago you described and explained the various relations and relationships between commanders; in other words, the Main Staff commander and the corps commanders. So my question is this: Since you were an assistant commander both in the Main Staff and at corps level, can you tell us whether the assistant commander at the Main Staff could issue orders to assistant commanders at corps levels? In other words, did they have command ability or capability?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you issue an order to someone who came to replace you at the 2nd Corps once you were transferred to the Main Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: All I could do is seek information from him, but I could not issue commands to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And could that person send any requests to you directly and sign them himself, personally, so could that be done in that way or what was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, that person would not be able to send any requests to me without his commander's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just, sorry for the interruption, but we repeatedly are getting the -- Mr. Skrbic working for the 2nd Corps. Somehow 2nd Krajina Corps is getting left out of it, and given that who we know the 2nd Corps is, I think it's probably an issue of speed, but I just wanted to point that out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We will resolve that. I will put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, did any organ within the corps have the capability to send any request to you, even if it was dealing with the same issues that they dealt with at the corps level as the issues that you dealt with at the Main Staff level, and could they sign such requests?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my purview usually the issues that I dealt with were proposals for promotions, and such requests could not be sent by an assistant commander at the 2nd Krajina Corps without the signature of the commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Now my next question: If an organ from within your sector were to be sent per order of the commander to a lower level unit at the brigade level or so, would you be able to issue orders to such an individual? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And would that person be allowed to send reports to you if he was acting in -- if he was acting according to the orders from the commander who was sent? So could he send reports to someone from your sector?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Regardless of who it was who was at my sector, who it was that sent him, the person --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat this part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you for a moment. We have two problems: One is that you are speaking quite fast, like Mr. Tolimir does sometimes, too, and you are overlapping. Please pause between question and answer. The interpreters have to finalise their interpretation, otherwise they will not get the first part of your answer. Could you please repeat the whole answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. So far I've tried to slow down, and I don't know why I picked up speed. Perhaps because the question was a very broad one, so I was just trying to save some time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. I will try to be brief in my questions and clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I asked the witness to repeat his answer and I would like to hear the answer. Please repeat the last answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All those who were transferred to units or were sent there in order to perform an analysis of the situation are duty-bound to assess the situation within their line of service. So those who were within the unit and who dealt with issues belonging to the same purview would report to them, and then this information would be collated and reported to the commander who sent them to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, the individuals who were sent to a lower-level unit, corps or brigade, either independently or as part of a team, who was it that they had to submit reports? Was it to the commander or to someone else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: They had to report -- to submit reports to their commander alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the next question: If someone from your sector, a person who was your subordinate, was sent to carry out a task from another purview that had nothing to do with mobilisation, for instance, but at a lower level, corps or brigade level, did that person have to report to you on any matters and was it their duty to send written reports to you on their work, on the task that they were assigned to perform? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't have to do that. But I would like to make a distinction here. If a commander assigned an individual from my sector to carry out another task, another assignment, he does not -- he was not obliged to inform me of that; however, if that individual was sent to carry out an assignment which was within my purview, that field, then they would have to report to me and inform me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And was he supposed to report during the task or following a task -- following a completion of the task?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Following the completion of the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So he would have to report on whose orders he performed that task as well, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, could you issue any orders or could you issue commands to an assistant corps commander for organisation, personnel, and mobilisation without the approval of the commander from the Main Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are quite a number of jobs that have to be done within my sector that run on a continuous basis, and people who were in charge of these areas knew ahead of time what it was that they were supposed to do. However, I could not take any steps that had to deal with the corps without the approval of the commander from the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you please explain just briefly what the difference is between the sector, an administration, and an institution or institute at the level of the main corps -- Main Staff and the corps levels? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Sectors or departments were complex units. They are more complex than administrations because their purview was broader. Administrations are of somewhat lower level rank than sectors or administrations because the volume of work that they had to do was less. And then you asked me about the institutes. Those are organisational units within the VRS that dealt with civilian affairs or semi --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Semi-civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for the needs of the VRS, some of which or some of whom were part of the VRS. And if you would like me, I can provide some examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please then answer my question that I am going to put now, and then you can give us some examples. Now, tell us -- now, could there be the same type of work or same jobs that would be assigned to various sectors; in other words, sectors that deal with various departments of work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Well, I am not really clear what you are trying to ask me, but can I try to clarify it, at least the way I understand it. Jobs of similar type are usually put within the same sector. They are assigned to the same sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it possible for a chief of sector or department to be a person who did similar work --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the question be repeated, please. It was not understood by interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters asked you to repeat your question because they didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The chief of sector, could he issue commands to all parts of his sector, administrations, units, and so on, or did he just unify them in terms of organisation or location?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect to General Tolimir, there was no chief of sector. There were assistant commanders for various areas. That was the official title in official documents. However, for ease of communication we can refer to them as chiefs, although such a title did not really exist. So an assistant in charge of a certain sector was responsible for the command and control of that sector, and then within the sector itself, the officers were his subordinates. But outside of the sector, no one was subordinate to him. The relationships within the sector itself were functional. For instance, General Djukic as the assistant commander for logistics could co-operate with another assistant commander, but we could not issue orders to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification and for the correction. But can you tell me, please, your organ or sector, could it be part of the rear organ or logistics organ that was under the command of General Djukic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, in our army was a distinction made between command and control, or, rather, "komandovanje, rukovodjenje i kontrola." Command, directing, and control. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, again this topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that everyone is aware of this problem. We do not have an exact interpretation because the semantics are different. So we have different terms. We have the word "komandovanje," "command"; "rukovodjenje," "direction"; and "kontrola," "control."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, it's, of course, a problem to have different languages in our record but it is taped and it might be checked at a later stage which words were originally spoken and which translation was used. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I don't want to bring up the old dispute, but CLSS has translated "komandovanje" and "rukovodjenje" as "command" and "control," and the term "kontrola" also is "control," not as "direction" as Mr. Gajic would prefer it. And so as long as we understand that, I think we can go ahead, but that -- that's the situation, the old debate which we obviously won't resolve here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is why I say on page 39, line 1, I didn't ask Mr. Gajic to help. I said "again this topic," with a question mark, because we indeed have had this discussion quite often. Mr. Gajic, you want to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just in order to be clear for the record, I spoke in Serbian and I mentioned the terms that Mr. Tolimir mentioned, and I was very careful not to say anything that might be understood to be leading to the witness or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this witness is capable to describe his position and his duties in the VRS properly, and this is the reason why I would like to put a question to him. Mr. Skrbic, you explained earlier today that there is a distinction between command and control. Did you have a control function in your position as assistant commander in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for making it easier for me to answer this question, because I know exactly what my purview was and what my responsibilities were. As far as my relationship with subordinate units, I had no control -- no command responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like really to clarify and to make a distinction between command and control. I just asked you about your -- if you had a control function.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had a supervisory function, not control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you explain that? What is the difference between supervisory function and control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A control entity had the right to take action and measures when something was established, a situation was established. As for supervision, that only meant that we would observe how certain actions are carried out. Control mainly had to do with command and combat tasks; whereas supervision had to do with personnel issues, security issues, logistics issues, and so on. Your Honour, we were duty-bound to have -- for instance, as assistant commander, I had to have insight into how certain orders for appointments were carried out, how orders to do with relief of duty were carried out, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: By carrying out this duty, it could happen that you find out that somebody is not following the correct procedure and is not abiding by orders. What are you doing then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would report that to the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If somebody in your sector is not abiding by any order, what are you doing then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there were no situations like that, but if somebody who was directly subordinated to me, there were measures that I could take then, but only in terms of reprimanding them. I was not entitled to dismiss them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Up to now we are dealing with the supervisory tasks, now we come to control. Did you personally or did your sector have any control function in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honours, only within the teams appointed by the commander of the Main Staff in order to dispatch them to carry out control of subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you have any command function in the VRS, inside your sector or to other units or subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within my sector I was superior to the officers appointed to that sector. Apart from that, I was not superior to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I asked you if you had command function of any kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was your deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Stojan Malcic was my deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was it possible that you did order him to do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I asked you if you had command function of any kind, and then you said "no," but you had command function in relation to your deputy. To whom else could you issue any kind of orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's this distinction that apparently cannot be properly established in our communications because there is still difference between command and control. It was possible for me to issue orders to Colonel Slobodan Kovacevic who was one of my subordinates, as well as to Stojan Malcic, but command function has to do with the carrying out of combat missions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I was just asking you about your command function you carried out personally, and you gave an answer. You were in a position to issue orders to your deputy and to subordinates in your sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was in a position to issue orders to a subordinate unit, in the corps or somewhere else, which was responsible for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs? For instance, in a corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the commander of the Main Staff issued orders to the corps commander within the relevant domain. I was not entitled to issue any corps orders of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not to any organisation in a subordinate unit which was responsible, for instance, for mobilisation or personnel affairs? How about promotion or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single unit. All I could do, Your Honour, was to intervene if they failed to submit proposals for promotion in time and just to remind them that they were supposed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the personnel organs from subordinate units, from the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that a supervisory function, when you find out that they failed to report, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We can agree that this constitutes a supervisory function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Or was it a control function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we are -- or I am struggling with this English terminology because in the Serbian language we distinguish between "supervision" and "control," and we see control as a more serious process which implies an imperative nature. Supervisory is a more lenient process and doesn't contain any imperatives. This is a distinction that I find difficult to explain for those who speak English. If there is no other term in English for supervision, then we can agree about control. But I explained to you what was the scope of control and what was the scope of supervision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When you found out that a subordinate unit didn't report correctly, could you order them to report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had the right to send the report back to them, pointing out the mistakes and asking them to correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers. Mr. Gajic, you wanted to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there was a mistranslation on page 42, line 15. It says here "command and control," whereas the witness was talking about the difference between command function and issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is your position. We have it on the record. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, since we didn't discuss much the function of control, was it possible for you to control the jobs that you assigned independently or were you able to control the jobs that were assigned to be done by units by the commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, two terms: "Control" and "control," or "rukovodjenje" and "kontrola," are often translated from B/C/S into English by using a single term, "control." Therefore, we have a slight confusion, and I believe that this is affecting both the witness, the Chamber, and all of us who are following this because if different terms are interpreted by one and the same word, which is "control," and due to that we wouldn't be able to read the transcript properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I am afraid that we will waste time to discuss that over and over again. We have received some advice by the translation unit, and we should be very much looking forward to overcome that. We can't resolve this problem in the courtroom, and everything is taped in all languages, so that might be controlled later on. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. On another topic, Mr. President. We see from this question where General Tolimir says: "And we didn't discuss much the function of control. Was it possible for you to control the jobs that you assigned independently or were you able to control the jobs that were assigned to be done by units of the commander?" Can we -- so the question is not vague and is understandable, when asked such a question, can he make sure he's telling us is he asking about directions to his staff within his sector, or is he asking about directions or directives or orders to his functional subordinates, those in the corps or the brigade. It's a completely different answer, and unless we know who he is issuing the directions to, we don't -- we won't -- the answer won't make any sense. And in that question you can't tell whether it's his sector he's issuing these things to or a corps or a brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir may clarify this if he wants to do it, otherwise you will have the opportunity to do that during your cross-examination, Mr. McCloskey. Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is not the first time in this trial that we came across this problem. If I remember correctly, we have had a similar instance last year, sometime in early autumn. We at that point in time asked the translation unit to check and revise the transcript and the tapes again and provide us with the correct official translation. We are not able to understand the B/C/S language. Mr. Tolimir is not able to understand fully English. Mr. Gajic is quite capable of English, but he is not an translation expert. Mr. McCloskey is not able to understand B/C/S, although I was deeply impressed when you used these terms. The only way to resolve this is after this -- after court, to ask the Registry and the translation unit to check the tapes in B/C/S and to revise the transcript of the testimony of this witness and to get an official revised version of the transcript. We, at least I, don't see any other way to resolve this problem without a waste of time. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, there may be some changes in interpretation, so please give us a precise answer about combat activities. Did assistant commanders control the business in their sectors in accordance with the commander's decision, or are they entitled to change it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: They cannot change it, but what they -- actually, what they cannot change is the commander's order; whereas a decision is part of an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me repeat my question: Can they change the commander's decision or order? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: They cannot change either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can they control the business or tasks in order to achieve what the commander ordered? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: They are experts for the implementation of the commander's order and decision in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that they can only engage in their professional business in the framework of the order or -- and -- given or task assigned to them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they can only engage in their professional business, their professional tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before this correction, please tell us what the closest synonym is of the B/C/S term "rukovodjenje"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: There is no complete synonym for "rukovodjenje." I said at the outset that sometimes "komandovanje" and "rukovodjenje," "command" and "control," are synonyms. They are compatible, but there are distinctions that must be born in mind. Whereas the term "rukovodjenje" has no synonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a synonym for "komandovanje," "command"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: There is a synonym. Oftentimes the term "issuing orders" is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a synonym for "kontrola" that would correspond to some of the activities carried out in the framework of command and control?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian language there is no synonym for "kontrola."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Let us not dwell on this any longer. Please take a look at the schematic that you see in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's Exhibit 2227.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It shows the structure of the Main Staff and staff unit. Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me just put on the record that on page 48, lines 4 and 7, it should read "kontrola." Now it's correct on the record. I hope we all can agree. Now continue please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see -- or, rather, enlarge this schematic because it's very small on my screen.
